source: Markovits, Brunet, Thompson & Brisson (2013) Direct evidence for a dual process model of deductive inference. JEP:LMC 39(4) 1213-1222 (abstract via Europe PMC; full text paywalled)
finding: Two experiments on the 50% vs 90% diagnostic. Exp 1: people under time pressure used the statistical pattern more, then switched to the counterexample pattern when time limits were removed. Statistical responding took less time than counterexample responding. People who started with free time preferred counterexample and kept it when later put under time pressure. Exp 2: people under pressure were less confident in the statistical than in the counterexample strategy and were more likely to switch when time was freed.
numbers: Abstract gives no sample sizes, no time limit in seconds, no percentages. Those numbers are still unopened, so gap 4 stays partly open.
quote: time pressure disrupts the ability to make good metacognitive choices
limits: Abstract only. The argument that capacity is not the cause rests on the order asymmetry (free time first, then pressure: counterexample kept). One lab. 'Switch' is inferred from two diagnostics given to the same person, not from process data.
agent_relevance: A fast, cheap, statistical mode and a slow counterexample-search mode are both reachable by the same reasoner. Under a hard token cap expect the estimate pattern, not search. A confidence signal on the fast answer predicts a switch to search (see d11).

source: Markovits & Thompson (2023) Can we change how people reason? Effects of instructions to reason differently and reasoning strategy. JEP:LMC 49, 1773-1785 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Two studies, 885 participants in total, gave explicit instructions to reason by counterexample or by probability. How well people followed the instructions was limited by their spontaneous strategy. The instruction effect carried over to two later tasks: belief-biased inferences (Study 1) and base-rate judgments (Study 2). Following the instructions correlated with accuracy on both tasks.
numbers: N = 885 across two studies. Per-study N, group sizes, effect sizes and transfer size are not in the abstract.
quote: the ability to follow these instructions was constrained by people's spontaneous strategy use
limits: Abstract only. Transfer is to the next task in the same session, so durability is untested. The review (d03) says Statistical reasoners changed most and Counterexample reasoners changed little.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 5: strategy can be steered by plain instruction, but the steer works best when it matches the existing default. An instruction 'reason by counterexample' may fail against the model's own default. Test it per item class instead of assuming it works.

source: Markovits (2024) Are There Two Kinds of Reasoners? J. Intelligence 12(3):25. Re-read of section 6 (How invariant are strategies?) and the conclusion
finding: The review's account of the 2013 and 2023 studies. 2013: a time constraint first gives a much higher share of Statistical strategies. After unlimited time first, then a constraint, Counterexample reasoners stay stable and some Statistical reasoners produce a Counterexample pattern. In a second study, confidence in the constrained strategy predicted keeping it later. 2023: after an initial diagnostic, people got one of two training procedures, then two sets of updating problems (from the 2015 paper) as a check, then belief-biased problems (Study 1) or base-rate problems (Study 2). Counterexample reasoners found counterexample instructions easier. Statistical reasoners found probabilistic instructions easier. Statistical reasoners who followed instructions changed their later performance, Counterexample reasoners changed little. The direction of change differed between belief-bias and base-rate problems.
numbers: No sample sizes, percentages or effect sizes for 2013 or 2023 appear in the review. It calls strategy a stable short term individual difference and says results hold at least in the very short term.
quote: strategy use, though relatively stable in the short term under normal conditions, is not invariant
limits: Secondary source. It also says people sometimes alternate strategies in successive judgments. No retest interval longer than one session is reported.
agent_relevance: The review itself marks the missing piece for gap 3: nothing covers stability across days or content sets. Treat any strategy label for the agent as a within-run measurement only.

source: Thompson & Markovits (2021) Reasoning strategy vs cognitive capacity as predictors of individual differences in reasoning performance. Cognition 216:104866 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Four studies of about 200 people each tested belief bias, base-rate neglect, conjunction fallacy and denominator neglect. Each person also did the strategy diagnostic plus IQ, cognitive reflection and numeracy measures. In three of four studies strategy predicted performance after the other measures were removed. For the conjunction fallacy, Bayesian analysis found that none of the individual-difference measures predicted a meaningful part of the variance. Strategy was a strong predictor on the other three tasks.
numbers: 4 studies, N about 200 each (about 800 in all). Effect sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Same lab. Correlational. Strategy is measured once per person in the same session as the task.
agent_relevance: Item-class answer for gap 6: strategy matters for belief-conflict, base-rate and denominator items, and does not matter for the conjunction fallacy. A router should not expect a strategy effect on every item class.

source: Markovits, Brisson & de Chantal (2017) Logical reasoning versus information processing in the dual-strategy model of reasoning. JEP:LMC (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Counterexample reasoners might simply be more sensitive to logical form. To test this, four studies used modus ponens (MP). Studies 1 and 2 gave MP with explicit statistical premise strength: Statistical reasoners accepted MP more often than Counterexample reasoners. Studies 3 and 4 used natural MP premises with many disabling conditions: the opposite pattern appeared. The authors conclude that the strategies are information-processing styles, not degrees of logic.
numbers: Per-study N and acceptance rates are not in the abstract.
quote: these strategies must be defined in terms of information processing
limits: Abstract only. This qualifies K02 (groups answer alike on MP): they answer alike on simple MP but diverge when premise strength is stated or disabling conditions are many.
agent_relevance: Do not map counterexample search to 'more correct'. Search helps where a falsifying case exists and can hurt where the premise is statistically strong. Item class decides.

source: Markovits, Lortie Forgues & Brunet (2012) More evidence for a dual-process model of conditional reasoning. Memory & Cognition 40:736-747 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Two studies gave sequences of affirmation-of-the-consequent inferences whose statistical properties differed, either stated or implied. Individual response patterns showed two distinct strategies. The counterexample strategy went with higher abstract-reasoning scores, and explicit counterexample information helped it. A further study with explicitly probabilistic inferences found that most people made statistically appropriate inferences, and more accurate ones went with higher abstract reasoning.
numbers: No N in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. This is the original diagnostic paper (a26 in the earlier pass was second hand).
agent_relevance: The diagnostic is built on response patterns across a block, not on one answer. Any LLM test needs a block of items and a pattern rule, not a single item.

source: Newman, Gibb & Thompson (2017) Rule-based reasoning is fast and belief-based reasoning can be slow. JEP:LMC 43 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Base-rate problems (Exp 1) and conditional inferences (Exp 2) were answered under a hard deadline, then again in free time. Fast answers were already informed by probability rules and logical validity. Slow answers added belief-based information.
numbers: No N or deadline in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Thompson also co-authors the diagnostic papers, so this is not a fully independent lab. It did not use the strategy diagnostic. It does show that fast answers are not simple guesses.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 4: a fast, capped answer carries real structure. A capped agent answer should not be dismissed as guessing, and a free-time answer can be worse on belief-conflict items.

source: Markovits, Bergeron & Gagnon-St-Pierre (2026) Thinking longer versus thinking better: Deliberation versus association. Memory & Cognition (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Study 1 (N=200) gave categorical syllogisms under 5 s pressure and with unlimited time. More time raised coherent normative responding and also raised responses linked to alternative generation. Study 2 (N=200) gave base-rate problems. More time lowered normative responding on Neutral problems (more deliberation) and on Conflict problems (more weight on the stereotype). People who improved in coherence with time resisted that decline.
numbers: Two studies, N=200 each. Effect sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Same lab. Shows that more time is not the same as more logic.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens more thinking can bring in associative content. A code check independent of the model's own long reasoning should guard conflict items, where extra deliberation can reinforce the lure.

source: Markovits, Thompson & Bergeron (2026) Fast reasoning uses semantic activation as an intuitive cue. Memory & Cognition (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Four studies used syllogisms of identical form where the major premise had Few or Many alternative antecedents, with two invalid forms (AC, DA) and one valid form (MT). Under severe time constraint people judged the conclusion invalid more often when the premise had Many alternatives than when it had Few.
numbers: Four studies. N and rates not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Same lab. Content differs, form is held constant.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap pre-reasoning signal: how many alternatives come to mind. A router could copy this item-level cue (count of easily available alternatives) to decide between estimate and search (gap 9).

source: Markovits (2025) Evidence for some form of abstract logical intuition. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Two studies gave people 5 s per inference. Items included semi-abstract syllogisms 'All A are B, X is B, X is A' with an abstract B term, with matching and semantic activation controlled. About 15% of people responded logically on these consistently.
numbers: About 15% consistent logical responders at 5 s; two studies.
quote: about 15% of participants were able to consistently respond logically to these inferences
limits: Abstract only. Same lab. Small fraction.
agent_relevance: Under a severe cap most fast answers come from cues (matching or semantics) and only a minority from form. This supports forcing a form check in code on invalid-looking AC or DA items (K16).

source: Thompson & Markovits (2025) Fast reasoning and metacognition. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: 289 people answered two blocks of belief-logic conflict syllogisms, the first under a time constraint and the second free. People with a mixed pattern under pressure and low Feeling of Rightness for belief-based answers shifted to validity-based answers when free. High-feeling people shifted toward belief-based answers. The feeling signal predicted both whether and in which direction an answer changed.
limits: Abstract only. Not about the diagnostic strategy directly. Same lab.
agent_relevance: Support for a cheap router (gap 9): a confidence-like signal on the first quick answer says whether to switch to search. A code rule on low confidence or low agreement across samples is the machine analogue.

source: Gagnon-St-Pierre, Doucerain & Markovits (2021) Reasoning strategies explain individual differences in social reasoning. JEP:General (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Three studies. Strategy predicted the self-serving bias (Study 1) and use of racist stereotypes even after need for closure was accounted for (Study 2). An essentialist prime raised gender bias among Statistical reasoners and had no effect on Counterexample reasoners (Study 3).
numbers: No N or effect sizes in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Same network. Item class is social judgment, not deduction.
agent_relevance: Item-class evidence for gap 6: the statistical default is the one most sensitive to priming and prior association. Context in the prompt may steer a model's default estimate the same way.

source: Markovits, Bergeron & Gagnon-St-Pierre (2026) Rethinking the nature of logical intuitions about deductive reasoning: Conflict detection and semantic cues. JEP:LMC; with Mekik, Vivier & Markovits (2026) A logical intuition based on semantic associations (JEP:LMC); abstracts via Europe PMC
finding: Three studies on 'All A are B, X are B': with premises that have many alternatives the intuitive judgment matches rejection, with few alternatives or an unfamiliar consequent it matches acceptance. The effect is not explained by formal validity or by a matching heuristic. Mekik et al. (two preregistered studies): confidence in accepting a believable conclusion was lower for many-alternative premises, and invalid few-alternative conclusions were liked more.
numbers: No N in abstracts.
limits: Abstracts only. All from the Markovits group. Competes with De Neys (2023, formal-validity intuition) and Ghasemi et al. (2022, matching).
agent_relevance: The intuition behind accept or reject on AC items is the availability of alternatives, which is what a counterexample search makes explicit. An agent can implement the same cue in code: the count of generated alternatives.

source: Poddar, Sahoo & Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives. arXiv 2512.12620
finding: 14 LLMs on 160 syllogisms (40 base items times content, nonsense and order variants; 76 valid, 84 invalid) under four prompts: zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot and zero-shot chain of thought, at three temperatures. Twelve of 14 models were more accurate on belief-congruent than on belief-incongruent items. Top models showed under 2 points of bias, weak models up to 46.9 points. Prompt effects were model-specific: no systematic gain from chain of thought. Few-shot lowered accuracy on average.
numbers: Mean belief bias +10.81 points (SD 16.32, p = .0280, d = 0.66). Bias vs performance rho = -0.565 (p = .0353). Few-shot mean change -3.57 points (p = .0165). 12 of 14 models positive.
limits: 14 models, 160 items. Majority vote of up to 10 samples. No validity-vs-likelihood framing and no strategy diagnostic.
agent_relevance: Plain chain of thought was not a reliable fix for belief conflict in this panel. Baseline for gap 2: any code-run search must be compared with plain chain of thought model by model, not on the average.

source: Hasan, Greff & Grissom (2026) Benchmarking LLM Competence on Logical Inference over Probability Operators. arXiv 2607.27405
finding: 14,320 generated prompts over fifteen inference templates (13 patterns, 10 valid and 3 invalid, in the main contrast) with five question forms (true, correct, valid, follows, direct), several negation styles and varied surface content. 29 models answered zero-shot with thinking off or at the lowest setting. Most had a fixed Yes or No preference that did not follow the logical form. Gaps up to 64 points appeared between negated and non-negated versions of the same question.
numbers: Only 9 of 29 models beat the 0.5 competence floor (Gemma4:31B 0.675, Sonnet 4.6 0.642, Opus 4.7 0.570). Eleven of 29 below 0.30. Affirmative-only floor correlates r = 0.90 with the full floor.
quote: Only 9 of 29 models exceed random chance.
limits: Direct-answer mode only, so no chain of thought or search. Task is epistemic modals (probably, must), not AC/DA with stated frequencies. All question forms are is-it-true/valid types, so there is no how-likely contrast.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence on gap 1 framing: models answer from a Yes/No prior more than from the logic, and question wording matters. A valid-vs-how-likely flip on the Markovits items is plausible but untested. Also a method point: score by a floor (worse of Yes-correct and No-correct), not by a mean.

source: Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima & Okada (2023) Evaluating Large Language Models with NeuBAROCO: Syllogistic Reasoning Ability and Human-like Biases. arXiv 2306.12567
finding: English and Japanese syllogism set with labels for belief, conversion and atmosphere. Atmosphere items are those where the right answer is neutral (nothing follows) but the quantifier types of premises and conclusion invite a yes. There are 104 such items. Models did far worse on them than on the average item.
numbers: Atmosphere items correct: RoBERTa 0%, BART 0.96%, GPT-3.5 39.42%. GPT-3.5 on consistent 61.05%, symbol 56.89%, inconsistent 31.37%. RoBERTa neutral-label accuracy 0.55%.
limits: Old models (GPT-3.5, 2023). No chain of thought contrast and no code probe. The atmosphere label is the authors' own rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the form-driven 'something follows' error is strong in weaker models and matches what a PHM min/atmosphere heuristic predicts. Whether a code-triggered 'nothing follows' probe fixes it without raising false rejections is untested.

source: Nguyen, Tachibana, Liu, Liu, Noe, Takeda & Kurohashi (2025/2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0: Japanese Benchmark for Belief-Inconsistent Syllogistic Reasoning. arXiv 2506.06955 v5
finding: All BIS items are logically valid but belief-inconsistent, so the right answer is always Yes. Reasoning effort mattered a lot for a small GPT-5 model and little or mixed for Qwen3-32B thinking mode.
numbers: BIS accuracy: GPT-5-mini (medium effort) 99.72, GPT-5-nano medium 98.84, GPT-5-nano minimum 69.22, GPT-4o 79.54, Qwen3-32B no thinking 99.58 vs thinking 99.12. NeuBAROCO belief-inconsistent: Qwen3-32B no thinking 94.01 vs thinking 97.60.
limits: Confound: every item is valid, so an always-yes bias scores perfectly. No invalid-believable items, so only half of the belief-bias design is tested. Effort levels are vendor settings, not equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 token budget: on belief-conflict valid items, low reasoning effort drops a small model sharply (69 vs 99), while for a strong model effort adds little. Budget sensitivity is model-dependent, and an all-valid design cannot show an accept-everything bias.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang & Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning. EMNLP Findings; arXiv 2305.12295 v2
finding: The LLM translates a problem into symbolic form and a deterministic solver does the inference. On average this beat chain of thought by 18.4 points and standard prompting by 39.2 points. It did not win everywhere: with GPT-4 on PrOntoQA chain of thought was better. When the symbolic form could not be executed, the system fell back on chain of thought.
numbers: GPT-4 (Standard / CoT / Logic-LM): PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20; ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. text-davinci-003 PrOntoQA 51.80 / 83.00 / 85.00.
limits: Forward inference by a solver, not counterexample search on invalid AC/DA or belief-conflict items. Tokens are not equalised and solver cost sits outside the token count. Chain of thought is the fallback.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: code-run reasoning beat plain CoT on four of five formal sets and lost on a simple set where the model already reached 98.8. The gain depends on translation quality, which the model controls. A code search needs a check that the formalisation is faithful.

source: Jha, Jha, Lincoln, Bastian, Velasquez, Ewetz & Neema (2023) Neuro Symbolic Reasoning for Planning: Counterexample Guided Inductive Synthesis using LLMs and Satisfiability Solving. arXiv 2309.16436
finding: A Z3 SMT solver checks the LLM's plan in blocks world and returns a counterexample, which goes back into the prompt. GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and older models were tried. Iterations needed were counted on 20 random problems with 3 and 4 blocks.
numbers: 20 random problems for the iteration analysis; a block-count sweep up to 6 blocks (GPT-3.5 correct-solution counts in a figure). No tokens-matched baseline.
limits: Very small. No matched plain-CoT arm in the parts read. Figure values were not recoverable from the extracted text. This is a code-judged counterexample loop on a planning class.
agent_relevance: Planning is a class where a code-run counterexample is natural because the checker is exact. It shows the loop is feasible, not that it beats chain of thought at equal tokens.

source: Zouak, Boukhalfa, Lakehal, Katiyar & Nefti-Meziani (2026) Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers: When Imitation Hurts and Reinforcement Repairs. arXiv 2610.02444
finding: 4,707 false undergraduate algebra and analysis conjectures, each with a Python verifier. Models often prove a true theorem forward but fail to disprove a close false one. Fine-tuning on counterexamples alone destroyed true-theorem recognition (0.27 to 0.00 for Qwen3-4B), and reinforcement learning with the verifier as reward repaired it (to 0.66). A human audit of 177 verifier decisions found 97.7% accuracy.
numbers: Qwen3-4B true-theorem recognition 0.27 to 0.00 after SFT, 0.66 after RLVR. Replicated over four seeds and on Gemma-3-4B. Sparse vs dense reward differ by 33 points on a held-out calibration probe. Verifier audit 97.7% of 177.
limits: Training study, not a prompting scaffold. Math conjectures, not conditional inference.
agent_relevance: Two lessons: a code verifier is cheap and accurate (97.7%), and pushing a model toward always-disprove damages its ability to confirm true claims. A counterexample step must not become an always-reject habit (false rejections).

source: Guo et al. (2026) Think When Needed: Model-Aware Reasoning Routing for LLM-based Ranking. arXiv 2601.18146 v2
finding: A light router head chooses between direct answer (Non-Think) and reasoning (Think) before generation, using only pre-generation signals: compact task features and model-aware difficulty signals from a diagnostic checklist. It beat Random and Self-select routing and always-Think at much lower cost. Removing either feature group lowered accuracy.
numbers: MovieLens, Qwen3-4B: +6.3% NDCG@10 using 49.5% of the tokens. MovieLens, Qwen3-8B N@10: Random 0.207, Self-select 0.209, router 0.216. Always-Think used about 8 times the tokens in one example (417 vs 55). Ablation on Amazon-VG, Qwen3-14B: trade-off 22.73 full vs 21.03 and 21.75 with a group removed.
limits: Ranking and recommendation, not deduction. The router is trained on labelled data. The model-asks-itself baseline did poorly, a warning for self-judged routing.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 analogue: a cheap pre-generation router beat random, self-selection and always-think on another task. For deduction no such test exists. Rule-based G1-style signals (alternative count, AC/DA form, conflict with prior) are untested candidates.

source: Search record: test-retest and long-interval stability of the strategy diagnostic (Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex attempts, web search; abstracts and the 2024 review text checked)
finding: No paper was found that reports a retest of the diagnostic after days or weeks, or across different content sets. The 2024 review calls strategy stable only in the short term. Within-session evidence exists: in 2013 Counterexample reasoners stayed Counterexample when pressure was added while some Statistical reasoners changed, and in 2015 a probability-first order moved later validity answers.
numbers: None. No reliability coefficient exists in anything opened.
limits: A negative search is weak. The 2013 and 2023 papers were read at abstract level only. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned rate-limit errors and the web search quota ran out.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a per-person or per-model type label as a stable trait in the scaffold. Re-measure within the run.

source: Search record: independent-lab replication of the Markovits diagnostic (Europe PMC queries on counterexample or statistical strategy papers, authors checked)
finding: Of the roughly 20 papers found that use the dual-strategy diagnostic, every one has Markovits or a close collaborator (Thompson, Brisson, de Chantal, Gagnon-St-Pierre, Beghin, Gratton, Bergeron) as an author. Related independent work tests neighbouring questions without the 50/90 diagnostic: Knauff and Gazzo Castaneda (2025, free-text justifications), Kosourikhina and Handley (2025, N=248, invalid AC/DA feel valid to many), Newman, Gibb and Thompson (2017, deadlines).
numbers: About 20 papers scanned. Zero independent replications of the diagnostic found.
limits: Search tool limits. A non-indexed or non-English replication could exist.
agent_relevance: The evidence for the construct rests on one network. Treat its effect sizes as upper bounds when designing agent tests.
